Strategic integration of Artificial Intelligence in urban services in Montreal, Canada In September 2024, the City of Montreal (Canada) adopted its “Artificial Intelligence Integration Strategy”, consolidating nearly a decade of experimentation into a single, coherent framework.

The city enjoys a world-class AI ecosystem, home to institutions such as the public research centre in AI called “Mila – Quebec AI Institute” and IVADO, and was among the first signatories of the ‘Montreal Declaration for a Responsible Development of AI’ in 2018.

Collaboration with European peers, including Amsterdam (The Netherlands), Hamburg (Germany), Milan (Italy) and Tampere (Finland), has helped refine technical approaches and align with emerging standards for urban digital twins and “Cityverse” development.
Rotterdam, together with Amsterdam and Eurocities, has created an algorithm registry to document AI systems, monitor risk levels and align with the EU AI Act’s transparency requirements.

Amsterdam (The Netherlands), for instance, since 2020 has instituted a public algorithm register ‘Algorithm Register Beta’, which requires municipal departments to document automated systems, create oversight mechanisms and ensure transparency and accountability across departments (OECD.AI Policy Observatory, 2023 [70] ).
The experience of Amsterdam (The Netherlands) suggests that AI literacy is not only required for citizens, but for municipal officials themselves.

places.name: Helsinki
snippets: The city of Helsinki (Finland) has introduced an AI-powered chatbot to assist residents in navigating rental housing services, offering 24/7 multilingual support while reducing the administrative burden on city staff (City of Helsinki, 2025 [49] ).

Tools such as UrbanistAI (Box 1), used in Helsinki and Dubai, apply generative AI to visualise citizen input, making complex land use scenarios easier to understand and debate (UrbanistAI, n.d. [22] ).

For example, Rotterdam and Helsinki employ geospatial, cadastral and satellite imagery data, alongside housing market information, to monitor housing developments, predict pricing trends and improve city service responsiveness.

In procurement, the city requires algorithmic impact assessment for digital solutions deployed in the city. • Amsterdam (The Netherlands) and Helsinki (Finland) maintain public AI Registers where algorithms used by the city are inventoried and documented, including considerations about risk level, human oversight and fairness.

Participants integrate a European network of peers for knowledge exchange and peer learning on AI. • The city of Helsinki’s “AI ABC” course and the City of Suresnes’ hybrid AI-assisted contact centre illustrate how public administrations can combine human expertise with AI capabilities to enhance responsiveness while maintaining human oversight.

Partnering with academia is part of the city’s digital rights commitments (Cities Coalition for Digital Rights, 2025 [135] ). • The Helsinki AI register was co-developed by the City and Helsinki’s Centre for Data Science.
